issues.detail: The Hebrew 'עֶרְיָה תֵעוֹר קַשְׁתֶּךָ' means 'Surely bare/laid bare is your bow' (i.e., your bow is stripped/uncovered), but the Chinese '赤身露體必使你的弓顯露' adds '赤身露體' (naked body) as an agent causing the bow to be revealed, changing the subject/meaning. The Hebrew has no verb '使' (cause) and no separate 'body' concept; it is a passive/state statement about the bow.

The Hebrew 'שְׁבֻעוֹת מַטּוֹת אֹמֶר' means 'the oaths of the tribes, the word' (i.e., sworn oaths of the tribes/rods), but the Chinese '杖的誓言你話語細拉' renders 'מַטּוֹת' as '杖' (rod/staff) and 'אֹמֶר' as '你話語' (your words), adding '你' (your) which is not in the Hebrew, and the construct relationship is altered.

The Hebrew 'נְהָרוֹת תְּבַקַּע אָרֶץ' means 'You split the earth with rivers' (or 'rivers you cleave the earth'), but the Chinese '大地必有大河破裂' reverses the subject/object: it makes '大地' (earth) the subject and '大河' (great rivers) the object, whereas in Hebrew 'תְּבַקַּע' (you split) has an implied second-person subject (God) and 'אָרֶץ' is the object. The Chinese also adds '必' (surely) and '有' (have) not in the Hebrew.
